item.title: After 26 years, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nearly all measles cases have been in people who had not received the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. - Jayla Whitfield-Anderson/Reuters Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore. An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy. The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country. To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients. Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission. In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026. There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states. It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said. The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it. “Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated. Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived. In 2025 and 2026 , however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection. More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year. Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC , and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports. ‘Measles is back’ The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore. “This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.” But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported measles cases this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. - Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said. Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea. If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk. In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal. All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination. The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.” “Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added. Could the US regain its elimination status? Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it. Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978. Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO. In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission. That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces. Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status. Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it. “That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said. “So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/13/health/us-measles-elimination-status

item.title: Lauren Boebert loses House seat to Democratic challenger in Colorado
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In what had been considered Colorado's most Republican-leaning congressional district, incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert has been defeated by Democrat Eileen Laubacher. The Associated Press called the race on Friday afternoon. Laubacher received 48.8% of the vote (187,488 votes) to Boebert's 47.9% (184,047 votes), with 99% of the vote counted. Douglas Mangeris, a libertarian, received 3.3%, or 12,720 votes, per AP. Boebert, an outspoken gun rights activist, has served in Congress since 2021 and is considered one of President Trump's staunchest allies on Capitol Hill. Laubacher is a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral who was deployed in Afghanistan. She also served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden. Laubacher's victory adds Colorado's 4th District to the more than 40 Republican-held districts that have flipped to Democrats this midterm cycle, including two others in Colorado. In an interview with NewsNation on Thursday, Boebert blamed her impending loss on "so many different variables" that plagued Republicans across the country, including gas prices, the war in Iran and Congress's failure to address corruption in the U.S. political system. She also argued that she and other members of the right wing House Freedom Caucus "weren't heard" when they called for Congress to take action on a variety of issues that voters care about, including government surveillance and "fair elections." The result is indicative of the remarkable swing toward Democrats that took place in historically safe Republican districts across the country. Boebert, who relocated from Colorado's more-purple 3rd District in 2023, won by more than 11 percentage points the last time she was on the ballot. Who is Eileen Laubacher? Laubacher served 34 years in the U.S. Navy, working in a variety of intelligence and command positions, before retiring in 2024. Her father also spent his career in the Navy, reaching the rank of vice admiral. Her grandfather served as a Navy combat diver during World War II. Laubacher spent significant periods of her Navy career abroad, including a deployment to Afghanistan in 2009 and service in a senior role at the U.S. Embassy in India. Though she said she had frequently told people in her life that she would "never run for office," Laubacher opted to enter the race for Boebert's seat because she believed residents of Colorado's 4th District deserved "serious and honest representation" in Congress. Laubacher had reportedly been a Republican throughout much of her life before registering as a Democrat in late 2025. Her decision to switch parties, she said, was driven by her view that the Republican Party had become "nearly unrecognizable" to her. Laubacher's recent party swap became the subject of a lawsuit during the Democratic primary, with one of the other Democrats in the race attempting to prevent her from qualifying for the ballot. That effort failed, and Laubacher later secured the Democratic nomination. In terms of policy, Laubacher is firmly within the moderate wing of the Democratic Party. She supports strong immigration enforcement, tax cuts for the middle class and reducing the national debt. She placed a heavy emphasis on affordability throughout her campaign, including calling on President Trump to repeal tariffs that raise consumer prices and end the war with Iran. Boebert's tenure First elected to represent Colorado's 3rd District in 2020, Boebert quickly became one of the more vocal and recognizable members of the House Republican caucus. She has been a persistent critic of the "deep state" and was a staunch supporter of Trump's efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election. During her first year in the House, she introduced separate resolutions to impeach then-President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris over their handling of the U.S. military withdrawal from Afghanistan. In 2023, she was one of the key voices behind a leadership battle among House Republicans that was only settled when Kevin McCarthy was elected Speaker after 15 roll call votes. Later that year, she mounted a second unsuccessful effort to impeach Biden. Boebert's personal life drew scrutiny in September 2023 after she and a male companion were escorted out of a stage production of Beetlejuice for allegedly "vaping, singing, [and] causing a disturbance." Though she initially denied acting inappropriately, she later apologized for her behavior, saying that her actions "fell short of my values." Though Boebert won her first House race by a comfortable margin, she narrowly avoided defeat in her bid for reelection in 2022, defeating her Democratic challenger by just 546 votes. Prior to the 2024 election, Boebert switched her reelection bid to Colorado's 4th District, a region of the state considered "far more favorable to Republicans." The move proved effective in helping Boebert secure a comfortable victory in 2024. But the redder district was not enough to insulate her from the widespread Democratic gains across the country this year. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/lauren-boebert-loses-house-seat-to-democratic-challenger-in-colorado-195908438.html

item.title: U.S. reportedly offered little help as Singapore probed Nvidia chip shipments
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China . One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date. Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation. Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades. Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News. Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source. The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient. Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport. The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025. By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry. That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang. Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing. "The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week. Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed. A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country. Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned." Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector . The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement. The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China. The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025. "One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case. Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate. "Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jensen-huang-nvidia-alice-huang-singapore-investigation-china-chips/

item.title: Trump's midterm setback leaves some longtime supporters questioning MAGA's future
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
COLUMBUS, Ohio - The young Republicans had grown restless even before their disastrous election, tired of President Donald Trump, his war and his handpicked candidates. Now about a dozen members of Ohio State University College Republicans plopped down their backpacks for their first meeting since the election and pondered what was next. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Abraham Dixon, 20, used to identify with Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. But MAGA seemed synonymous with loyalty to Trump, and he'd come to think of Trump as "the anchor around the elephant's neck." He worried that even a politically diminished Trump would keep bending the party to his will - and compared him to the aging emperor villain of Star Wars. "He's Palpatine," Dixon said. It was hard to picture the GOP without the man who defined it for a decade. Trump's GOP was all they knew: Many cast their first votes for him. But chapter president Hunter Willmitch was blunt in an interview about the changes underway: "The MAGA movement, in my opinion, is dead." MAGA is certainly muddled, as its rank-and-file voters look to leaders outside of the Trump administration, have crossed over to Democrats or disengaged from politics altogether. There is no consensus about who should run in 2028 and plenty of skepticism for Vice President JD Vance, who once seemed the heir apparent. Like Trump or not, everyone agrees his vacuum will be hard to fill. Right-wing influencers increasingly critical of Trump were declaring themselves vindicated by his rebuke in the midterms. Extremists like Nick Fuentes, the white-supremacist influencer, saw the chaos on the right as an opportunity. "We could not have asked for a better outcome," Fuentes declared on his live stream. It was a moment of both peril and opportunity for the Ohio State College Republicans who held their meeting in an empty classroom one night this week. "How are you?" a young woman asked Willmitch as she sat down. "Upset at the amount of losses we took," Willmitch said. "Tuesday was rough," she said. "I thought it was going to be a little rough," Willmitch echoed. "I just didn't expect … that." He mentioned the bright spot in Florida, where Republicans had weathered the blue wave and Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was preparing another presidential bid. "If it's not for Ron DeSantis, that [state] probably flips," Willmitch said. He liked what he was hearing from the Florida governor, a longtime champion of the culture wars who now said Republicans needed to stop "fighting yesterday's battle" - prioritizing issues like the rise of artificial intelligence rather than pouring money into ads about transgender issues. Dixon agreed that the party's best bet was someone outside the Trump administration like DeSantis. He snorted when another student brought up Trump's latest interview on "60 Minutes," in which he suggested he wanted to compromise with Democrats on immigration. Republicans were like "a dog under the dinner table," the other student vented, told to be grateful for what Trump handed them. He wanted the party to run more staunch conservatives and talk more about the new populist issues animating both the right and the left: Flock cameras and data centers. Ohio state Rep. Brian Stewart (R), an Ohio State alumnus, was there as a guest speaker and was frank about the party's struggles this election cycle. Yes, Republicans were drawn into fighting old battles, he said, but "part of it too is we didn't have a lot of good things to say." A student asked him what the GOP should look like after Trump, and Stewart said Trump's overhaul of the party would endure in "the way we interact with the media, the way we sort of address questions, the way we sort of take criticism." "There used to be this just this defensive crouch that every Republican officeholder had," Stewart said - no longer. Yet Republicans couldn't just mimic Trump, he warned. The president had long defied political gravity, saying and doing things that other politicians would never get away with. He said other elected officials would need to abide by "a baseline of kindness and respectability." "We need voters to like us." A 'Front Row Joe' packs up Rick Frazier's living room was still plastered with mementos from his decade as one of Trump's "Front Row Joes" who followed him to rallies around the country. There was his picture with Trump, signed in gold pen. There was his photo with another Trump superfan best known as "Brick Suit." There was the framed letter he got from Trump in 2023 after his daughter died of a drug overdose. "Melania and I are devastated," the letter read. Frazier, 70, had thrown himself into the MAGA movement more fervently than almost anyone in the country, hooked from the moment Trump came down a golden escalator in 2015. Retired from a factory that made tank tracks for the military, he believed Trump would "drain the swamp" and help American industry. Now Frazier was done with him. From his couch in western Ohio, he laughed along at an episode of the comedy show "South Park," which has brutally and crudely skewered Trump and his administration over the past year. "He's the king of swamp," he said. Frazier's shift unfolded gradually, he said. He barely spoke about it with the other Front Row Joes - most of whom still adored Trump. He didn't like it when Trump resisted his supporters' push to release the government's full files on the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and he cringed when Trump, from the rally stage, mocked the word "affordability." He voted for Trump to straighten out the southern border and crack down on the drug trade that stole his daughter, and he couldn't make sense of Trump's decision last year to pardon a former Honduran president convicted for overseeing a "narco-state" that routed cocaine to the United States. "See, that got me all upset," he said, his voice wavering. His last Trump rally was in Kentucky, where the president railed against Rep. Thomas Massie (R), a rebellious Republican whom Frazier liked. When the midterms came, Frazier voted for his longtime Republican congressman Jim Jordan but also backed Democrats for governor and Senate, helping to flip Ohio blue. This week, he watched live as Massie unsuccessfully moved to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war with Iran. "I'm kind of going to go back to the way I was before Trump," Frazier said. "I was independently swinging wherever the best guy was running. And that's the way I think it should be. " Frazier still liked Vance, whom he's met, and thought the vice president was being honest about Republicans' missteps. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X the day after the midterm elections. But Frazier and plenty of other Trump voters were up for grabs now - and it wasn't clear who could turn him into a Front Row Joe again. 'Nobody worth voting for' At a chicken wing chain in southern Ohio, Heather Romine said she was raised to believe that you can't complain about things if you don't do something about it. So she cast a ballot in every election after she turned 18 - until last week. The 38-year-old conservative voted for Trump, but at some point in his second term, she just stopped following what was happening. "I can't keep up with it," Romine said at the bar, seated next to her boyfriend, who still liked Trump. "I don't want to keep up with it. It's defeating. It feels like it doesn't matter." "There's not a better candidate," her boyfriend said. "Nobody worth voting for," Romine replied. Her rural, working class community in Pike County, Ohio had swung harder to the right in the Trump era than almost anywhere in the country, embodying MAGA's rise. Voters heard Trump's outsider pitch and thought he would be different from other politicians. Now Romine struggled to say what could motivate her to vote again. Republicans won Pike County by a little more than 30 points last week compared to more than 50 points in 2024, in part because people stayed home. "I feel like I'm just a silent person on the sidelines right now, watching the ship burn," Romine said. She voted for Trump because she thought he would "get s--t done," but she felt she got chaos with tariffs and a war that upended the global economy. She owned a house and had a good job in health care, but with three kids, she still felt strained. She could spend $400 on a trip to the grocery store and lost track of how many times she helped buy food over the past year for a friend, a struggling single mother of two. She wanted the country to get back to something more like the "America First" vision Trump pitched - a sentiment others shared. "I think his America First agenda was a good idea, but I don't think he stuck to that," said Brandon Williams, a 46-year-old firefighter who voted three times for Trump. "So I would like to see somebody run somewhere on that same line, but actually do that." Plenty of people in town still supported Trump and thought he was doing the best he could. The war wasn't great, they said, but he closed the borders and pushed back on ideas about gender identity that disturbed them. They were all over the map, however, about who could follow Trump in 2028 and if MAGA would hold together. They were more familiar than most with Vance, an Ohio native who briefly represented the state in the Senate. But they often weren't sure about him and struggled to put their finger on why. "I just don't know, said Rick Patrick, 74, who prefers Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "It's a feeling." Diane Alley, a retired nurse, worried no one could recapture what Trump had stirred up here. "I'm terrified," she said as she made her way through the grocery store. "I don't know who they can run. Nobody is going to equal him." A White House spokesperson pointed to Trump's comments on "60 Minutes" that he thinks MAGA can continue without him. "Because MAGA is basically common sense … strong borders, good military," Trump said. But the president said Republicans would have done better last week if he were on the ballot, "because you saw the level of popularity and love." "There was love," he said. item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented summit as wars strain global relations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers. While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance. Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries. Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers. Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran . The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles. Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China . The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the “beginning of hopefully a conversation” on nuclear disarmament “that can be productive going forward,” said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced. But Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact. Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to “step up ... to the adult table” on a matter of international importance. Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades. More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran. The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. “You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said. The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.” Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi . Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022. As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies. In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine. Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan. Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia , waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war . Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back. Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others. “It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.” ___ Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow. item.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop after thousands of flight cancellations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Travelers wait for their luggage at Los Angeles International Airport on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/William Liang) AP Photo/William Liang The Federal Aviation Administration announced that the nationwide ground stop it issued earlier on Friday has been lifted, nearly five hours after thousands of flights were canceled across the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a press conference Friday night that the airspace has reopened and some flights have started to take off, but warned that "it'll be slow." "It's going to take us some time to unwind what happened this afternoon," he said. Duffy said that "instability" in the radar communications at air traffic control centers began just after 3:30 p.m. ET. At the time, there were more than 3,500 planes in the air when the ground stop was issued —he blamed it on an "incredibly old air traffic system." "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said. "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." He went on to blame Congress for not providing the funds to update the outdated infrastructure. "I can't build things if I don't have money," Duffy said. Last year Congress approved $12.5 billion to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on, including old copper wires and radio systems. On social media, the GOP-controlled Senate Commerce Committee, which oversees the FAA, noted that "no new" air traffic area control centers have been built "since [Lyndon B. Johnson] was in office." On Friday, Duffy asked for $50 billion from Congress to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. “This is bipartisan. This is American,” he said. He also didn’t rule out the possibility of another outage due to the “analog” system. “You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said. When asked if he could say with certainty that the problem wasn't caused by a cyberattack, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said, "There is nothing certain right now. It doesn't appear that way." Earlier in the day, Mullin told reporters that there was no reason to suspect a national security threat was behind the outage. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones," Mullin said. "This is not another 9/11," he added. "This is a telecommunications outage; this is much different." As news of the ground stop spread, Duffy wrote in a post on X , "The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." As of 9:30 p.m. ET, there were more than 25,100 flights delayed on Friday and more than 6,600 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.com , a live flight tracker website. There were more than 30,000 departures and arrivals scheduled for the remainder of the day, according to flight tracking app Flighty, the New York Times reported . Airlines for America, an industry trade organization representing major U.S. airlines, wrote in a post on X , "Safety is always our top priority." It added that it's in communication with the Department of Transportation and the FAA. The association encouraged travelers to be in touch with their airline carrier for "real-time updates." Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation into the nationwide ground stop. "The safety of our skies is built on redundancies," she wrote on X in response to Duffy's update. "Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation. As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I'll be demanding answers from the FAA." Citing multiple sources, CBS News reported Friday that "an update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage." It reported that the system is operated by L3Harris Technologies. The Wall Street Journal also reported that the outage appeared to be affecting the "telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies," which "handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots." Microsoft said that its own global outage — from which it is still recovering — did not appear to be a factor. Mullin also said they weren’t connected. The National Weather Service told the New York Times that a viral screenshot claiming that its weather radar is down is "outdated," adding that it "has not experienced a disruption to its radar systems today." Earlier this week, the FAA announced the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays. Called SMART — short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — it was made by an AI company called ASI and had previously been in use at Washington, D.C., airports since late September. On social media, ASI said, "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." A Yahoo reporter who was stuck on the tarmac on a United Airlines flight waiting to depart from Los Angeles International Airport passed along updates from the cabin. She said her pilot told passengers that "what happened was a communications outage that started in Kansas City Center, which is responsible for the airspace above the middle of America, and it spread nationwide." She also said she received an update from United Airlines, which said, "Air traffic control is limiting the number of planes allowed to land and depart each hour in Los Angeles, affecting several flights. We're monitoring the situation closely to get you to your destination as soon as possible." Around 7 p.m. ET, she said her flight "going over the Pacific" had departed. The New York Times has reported that "some international flights from the United States have been allowed to depart amid the ground stop." Alaska Airlines said in a statement that flights within Hawaii and Alaska have also been continuing, as have longer-distance flights to and from Honolulu. Nationwide ground stops are pretty rare. The last time such an event occurred was in January 2023, when a pilot notification system went down. Before then, a nationwide ground stop was issued following the September 11, 2001, attacks. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/faa-says-nationwide-ground-stop-is-over-after-thousands-of-flights-canceled-021133009.html

item.title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country. Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development. He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited among other issues a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service. Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents. “If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem-solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.” Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.” Three former governors including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father, also endorsed him. In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors. His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race. He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy. Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson's campaign was not immediately returned. Many Republicans saw ranking as their party’s best shot of retaining the governor's seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October. Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary. Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state. The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018. Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/kreiss-tomkins-becomes-first-democrat-050735181.html

item.title: White House seeks $50 billion to overhaul air traffic control after outage
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late Friday after a communications issue forced a nationwide groundstop that halted thousands of ‌flights for hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the White House earlier on Friday asked for $30.1 billion to ‌upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system. "This is an emergency," Duffy said. "What's more important than having an air traffic ​control system that actually works?" The issue impacted the FAA's en route centers that handle traffic between airports. But the Republican-led Senate Commerce Committee said the incident highlights the need to prioritize modernizing those centers over other projects and noted Congress approved $1.9 billion to replace outdated en route centers. The world's most complex airspace has experienced a series of events in recent years ‌that have disrupted flights and risked safety. ⁠In January 2025, a midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people. Congress already approved $12.5 billion over five years in July 2025 to upgrade air traffic control and ⁠increase the hiring of controllers following complaints about airport congestion, flight delays and technology problems. The request from White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy seeks $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, including $7.2 billion for ​a common ​automation platform and controller workstations and $2 billion for cloud computing. "This ​investment is critical to complete the modernization of ‌our national airspace - delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Vought wrote to lawmakers asking for swift action. Major airlines including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines have expressed support for the request. The $30.1 billion request also includes $2 billion to replace and improve Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control towers and $18 billion for airport-related projects including $10 billion to modernize or replace ‌aging terminals. The FAA relies on decades-old computers as well as replacement ​parts bought through auction websites. Last week, it said it would replace ​by the end of 2028 floppy disks used ​for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities. Vought and ‌Duffy in their letter said the FAA has ​replaced 68% of legacy copper telecommunications ​network with high-speed fiber infrastructure. The administration has called for the Republican-led Congress to approve funding in the final weeks of the year. Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January. In September, the dual ​failures of a circuit at a ‌Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental severing of a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a ​construction crew led to thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast being delayed or canceled. (Reporting ​by David Shepardson; Editing by Christopher Cushing and Shri Navaratnam) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/white-house-urges-congress-30-100226016.html
